help.title: Help
help.description: This overview explains how to get started in {{appName}} after you are already inside the app, plus the working styles that tend to work best.

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.step1: Start by creating a session and telling Claude Code or Codex what you want to accomplish.
gettingStarted.step2: If your work is tied to a codebase, select a working directory before asking it to read files, explain code, or make changes.
gettingStarted.step3: Treat the chat area as a persistent work thread: ask for work, inspect results, and keep iterating from there.

workflows.title: Recommended workflows
workflows.description: {{appName}} works best when you split different goals into separate threads and switch between them from the sidebar.
workflows.item1: Explore first: ask the agent to explain the project structure, key files, and constraints before changing code.
workflows.item2: Ship in small steps: ask for narrow edits, review the results, then keep iterating until the task is complete.
workflows.item3: Parallelize when needed: create separate sessions when you want to isolate context for different goals.

recommendedWays.title: Recommended ways to work
recommendedWays.description: Describe the goal and the surrounding context first, then state the form of result you want. This usually works better than sending one short command alone.
recommendedWays.item1: Be explicit about what you want done, then add the relevant directory, files, or constraints.
recommendedWays.item2: Break large tasks into multiple turns: understand first, edit second, verify third.
recommendedWays.item3: Create a new session for independent problems instead of mixing everything into one thread.

linuxUpdates.title: Linux install and updates
linuxUpdates.description: Linux currently ships as a .deb for Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04. When a newer build is available, the app downloads it and asks for your system password to install.
linuxUpdates.item1: First install with sudo apt install ./cindy-<version>-<arch>.deb (amd64 on x64, arm64 on arm64).
linuxUpdates.item2: In-app updates download the .deb. After you choose Update, a system prompt installs it over the current package.
linuxUpdates.item3: Linux does not offer the beta channel or idle auto-install, because installing requires your password.

agentResource.title: Agent Resource Usage
agentResource.description: Limit how much system capacity Agent command-line work can consume, so parallel tests or builds don't freeze your machine. Defaults to full speed (no intervention). The concurrency limit applies immediately; priority lowering reaches running Agent processes within about 15 seconds; raising priority back to Normal and toolchain thread caps only apply to newly started Agent processes. Applies to local Agents only; Agents on remote (SSH) machines are not governed by these settings.

presetHints.full: No limits (default). Agents use the machine at full speed; when switching back from another profile, Agents already running only fully recover after they restart.
presetHints.balanced: Command queueing + lower priority + toolchain thread caps: Agents keep working while foreground apps always come first.
presetHints.background: Lowest priority (efficiency cores on macOS) + a strict concurrency limit: quiet and responsive, but Agents run noticeably slower.
presetHints.custom: Custom combination. Adjust the fields below directly.

agentResource.maxConcurrentHint: Maximum number of commands the Claude Code engine may run at once; extra commands wait in a queue. 0 means unlimited. Codex commands run inside their own sandbox without a per-command hook and are covered by the priority and thread-cap layers instead.
agentResource.priorityHint: Lower it so Agents only use idle capacity and foreground apps stay responsive. Raising it back only applies to newly started Agent processes.
agentResource.capThreadsHint: Injects environment variables such as VITEST_MAX_FORKS and MAKEFLAGS so a single test or build command can't take every CPU core. Variables you set yourself are never overridden.

page.createPrompt: I want to create a Cindy plugin. First call ghost_forge_guide to get the handbook's table of contents, read chapter 0 (design alignment) first, then read the relevant chapters via the section parameter (at minimum the capability overview, sandbox red-lines, and packaging chapters) before writing any code; do not start implementing yet. Begin by asking questions: prefer option-based question cards, one key decision per card with your recommended choice marked, and proactively surface design options I may not know about — such as the UI form (docked panel, panel inside the Plugins page, chat card, or no UI), a $ command word, launch mode, background abilities (event listening, in-app toast notifications, unread badges, confirmation dialogs), network access, whether a settings page is needed, whether a bundled Node process should do heavy lifting, and whether image/video media abilities are needed. Step by step, confirm the problem to solve, target users, interaction flow, required tools and connections, permission boundaries, and acceptance criteria. After I confirm the design, implement and validate it according to the specification, then call ghost_forge_pack to validate and produce the .cindy package; do not claim that it was installed.

guide.title: Custom Plugin Marketplace Guide
guide.intro: A plugin marketplace is a Git repository or local folder with a manifest file, used to distribute a set of Cindy plugins.
guide.structureBody: A marketplace needs one manifest file plus one directory per plugin. Every plugin directory must contain a valid ghost.json (the plugin identity card).
guide.structureNote: The manifest can live in one of these locations:
guide.manifestBody: name is the unique identity of the marketplace (you manage it by this name after adding). Each source in the plugins array points to a plugin directory inside the repository as a relative path; the object form {"source": "local", "path": "…"} is also supported.
guide.sourceBody: Accepted sources: GitHub shorthand owner/repo, full Git URLs (https / ssh / git@), and local folder paths (~ supported). Git ref accepts a branch, tag, or commit; leave empty for the default branch. Sparse paths (one per line) check out only the listed subdirectories — useful for large repositories.
guide.authBody: Authentication relies entirely on your system Git configuration — Cindy never stores Git credentials. SSH: a working key must be configured on this machine; if the organization enforces SAML SSO, authorize the key for that organization via Configure SSO in your GitHub SSH key settings. HTTPS: use a Personal Access Token stored by the system credential helper.
guide.rulesBody: Plugin ids are globally unique, first come first served — conflicts with installed plugins are called out explicitly. Plugins whose ids use the official reserved prefixes ({{reservedGhostIdPrefixes}}) cannot be installed by dragging in a package, choosing a file, or using a custom plugin marketplace. Declared permissions are shown on the detail page; clicking Install completes installation and enables the plugin without another permission confirmation dialog.

perm.cindyTextOneshot: Can ask Cindy's fast lane a question and receive a text answer
perm.cindyTextOneshotDetail: Uses the system's lightweight utility model chain (the same lane as auto titles). No Agent involved and no file access. Model charges may apply.
perm.cindyEmbedText: Can send text to be turned into vectors (for semantic search)
perm.cindyEmbedTextDetail: Text is sent to the system embedding model and turned into numbers, up to {{max}} items per call. Model charges may apply. The vectors go only to the plugin — nothing is written to your own library.
perm.cindySearchWeb: Can search the public web with Cindy AI
perm.cindySearchWebDetail: Search requests access the public web and may consume Cindy AI quota.
perm.cindyTextOneshotModelDetail: Uses the system's lightweight utility model chain (the same lane as auto titles). No Agent involved and no file access. Model charges may apply. The plugin declares a preferred model: {{model}} (effective when available in the current catalog; your pin takes precedence).
perm.agentUserAction: Can start a new Agent turn after you click a plugin card
perm.agentUserActionDetail: Each click permits one turn only, and only in the session that owns the card.
perm.agentBackground: Can automatically start new Agent turns in the background
perm.agentBackgroundDetail: Does not require a click each time, but can only use sessions you previously connected to this plugin. Model charges may apply.
perm.agentErrand: Can hand tasks to the Cindy Agent and collect the result
perm.agentErrandDetail: Tasks run in this plugin's dedicated session, always visible in the sidebar and stoppable at any time. Read-only by default; raising the level requires your change in the plugin settings. Model charges may apply.
perm.agentSchedule: Can ask you to create an automation
perm.agentScheduleDetail: It can only open the new-automation panel with the fields filled in; whether it is created is up to you — pick a model and save it yourself. Once created, Cindy runs it on the schedule you set. Model charges may apply.
perm.nodeRuntime: Can run a bundled Node program on this computer
perm.nodeMcp: Can run a bundled stdio MCP on this computer
perm.nodeRuntimeDetail: High risk: it has the same local access as your user account, including files, network, and starting other programs. Cindy cannot contain it in the browser sandbox.
perm.nodeSecret: Can provide the stored credential “{{name}}” to the local Node program
perm.nodeSecretDetail: Cindy stores it encrypted and injects it only while the declared Worker methods below run. The Node program receives the plaintext and can return, log, save, or otherwise expose it to browser-side plugin code or Agent parameters. Only install plugins you trust.
perm.nodeResident: The Node program can stay running in the background
perm.nodeResidentDetail: Runs while the plugin is enabled and stops when disabled, updated, uninstalled, or when Cindy exits.
perm.panelLeft: Panel "{{title}}" · docked left of the chat
perm.panelTab: Panel "{{title}}" · opens inside the Plugins page
perm.mainView: Can add a “{{title}}” entry to Cindy's sidebar
perm.mainViewDetail: Opening it displays the main view in the plugin sandbox and does not grant file, network, or credential access.
perm.codeDetail: Runs in an isolated sandbox with no access to your files or network.
perm.resident: Always-on (starts when enabled, keeps a background process even when idle)
perm.residentDetail: Uses a small amount of memory while idle; the process stops immediately when it is disabled or uninstalled.
perm.subscribeTopics: Observes your session activity (turn and session events, no message content)
perm.subscribeActivity: Observes when the AI is thinking and when it is waiting on you
perm.subscribeActivityDetail: Sees only the timing: when thinking starts and ends, and when the AI is waiting for your approval or your answer. It never sees the reasoning text, the action awaiting approval, the command or file involved, the plan, the question, or your answer — and it cannot approve anything on your behalf.
perm.subscribeHooks: Can read, block, or rewrite the messages you send
perm.subscribeHooksDetail: Reviews each message before sending: it may block it or rewrite the text before it goes out; blocked messages can be edited and resent.
perm.subscribeAssistantReply: Can read and rewrite the AI's replies
perm.subscribeAssistantReplyDetail: Processes each AI reply after it completes: it may polish or rewrite the text (replacing it directly, without keeping the original), or replace the reply bubble with its own rendered card (in that case the original text is kept and can be viewed with one tap).
perm.cardExternalLink: Cards may declare external links that open your browser after confirmation
perm.cardExternalLinkDetail: Clicking a card link shows a confirmation dialog; the URL opens in your system browser only after you approve. Only http/https addresses are allowed.
perm.notify: Can show system tips (light banner at the top of the screen)
perm.notifyDetail: Tip text is provided by this plugin and labeled with its name; tips fade automatically and never block your work.
perm.badge: Can light an unread mark on the Plugins entry
perm.badgeDetail: When it has something new, it can show a green dot on the sidebar Plugins entry and on its own card, with a one-line summary. Opening its panel clears the dot. The dot makes no sound, does not vibrate, never reaches your system notification center, and is a permission separate from system tips.
perm.confirm: Can ask for your confirmation in a dialog
perm.confirmDetail: Before acting it can open a dialog that looks like Cindy's own to ask you. The question comes from the plugin and the dialog is labeled with its name; only you can click confirm or cancel — the plugin cannot. At most one dialog at a time, and asking too often is blocked.
perm.fsWriteDetail: Its own private data folder is always writable. Writes into the current session's working directory follow the session's permission mode (auto-approve modes write directly; per-action modes ask you first). Any other folder always requires your confirmation. Files are always written by the host — the plugin itself never touches your file system.
perm.libraryPersist: Can use a durable library (large files and databases)
perm.libraryPersistDetail: It gets a Cindy-managed storage area for your work (canvases, images, databases) with no normal plugin data quota. All file and database operations are executed by the host; the plugin only uses relative paths inside its own library and cannot touch your other files. Uninstalling the plugin does not delete this data; deletion requires separate confirmation in Cindy settings.
perm.networkSecretGhostInputDetail: Collected by this plugin's own settings UI — the plugin page sees the value at entry time. It is then handed to the host in one step for encrypted storage; once stored, the plugin can never read it back, and the host injects it only for the domains it declares.
perm.networkSecretIdentity: Will use your login email as the credential "{{name}}"
perm.networkSecretIdentityDetail: The value comes from your signed-in account's email, derived and injected by the host at request time; nothing to fill in. The plugin can read this email to show the current identity in its settings UI.
perm.networkSecretGhCli: Will prefer your local GitHub CLI login for the credential "{{name}}"
perm.networkSecretGhCliDetail: The host reads the local gh login token only when needed and injects it only into GitHub API requests; plugin code cannot read or store the token. If gh is unavailable, you can configure a fallback Personal Access Token in the plugin settings.
perm.networkSecretOrganizationIdentity: Will use your Cindy organization identity as the credential "{{name}}"
perm.networkSecretOrganizationIdentityDetail: Cindy issues a short-lived identity assertion when needed, and the host sends it only to the explicitly listed service hosts. The plugin code cannot read or store the token.
perm.networkSecretOauth: Will guide you through OAuth authorization at {{host}} ({{name}})
perm.networkSecretOauthDetail: The authorization flow and all tokens are managed by the host and can never be read by the plugin code; you provide the client credentials on the plugin detail page. The requested permission scopes are listed verbatim below — review them before approving.
perm.networkConnections: Can connect to {{label}} addresses you add
perm.networkConnectionsDetail: Addresses are added in this plugin's settings UI; every new address requires your confirmation, and the credential you provide is injected only for its own address.
perm.codeDetailNetwork: Runs in an isolated sandbox with no access to your files; network access is limited to the domains listed above, relayed by the host.
perm.codeDetailWithNode: The panel UI runs in an isolated sandbox; local processing is provided by the Node runtime declared above.
perm.pick: Can ask you to pick a folder for it
perm.pickDetail: When it asks, Cindy shows the system folder picker; you decide what to share, and cancelling gives it nothing.
perm.workspace: Can ask to create a session entry for a project folder in the sidebar
perm.workspaceDetail: When it asks, you either pick the folder yourself or see the full path on a confirmation card before deciding; while it is handling a call you started, subfolders inside the current session's working directory are used directly without an extra prompt. Folders that already have a session are reused, and what gets created is an empty session — nothing starts running on its own.
perm.sessionContext: Can learn which project folder the current session is working in
perm.sessionContextDetail: Shares only location facts (session ID and project folder path) while it works for the current session — no file contents, and no file access is granted.
perm.preview: Can open preview pages from the sites below in the sidebar browser
perm.previewDetail: Only the sites listed below can be opened; every page it opens is attributed to this plugin.
perm.iosSimulator: Can view the current task's embedded iOS Simulator status and open its controls
perm.iosSimulatorDetail: The Cindy Host still owns simulator lifecycle, WDA, Native Sidecar, video, and input. The plugin receives no frame bytes, input privileges, native Helper access, or IDs from other tasks.
perm.nodeChildSpawn: Its Node program can ask the host to start declared sub-processes from its package
perm.nodeChildSpawnDetail: Only JS files declared inside its own package can be started (same local permissions as the main program); arbitrary commands cannot be executed. Sub-processes are closed together when the plugin is disabled or exits.
perm.skill: Adds the skill "{{name}}" to your AI assistants
perm.skillDetail: A skill is an instruction file the AI loads and follows as its own, with your full permissions, in Claude Code and Codex, across every project — it is not confined to this plugin's sandbox. It stays available while the plugin is enabled and is removed when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled; turning the plugin off for a single folder does not hide it. The full skill text cannot be previewed here — only install plugins you trust.

nightly-test-heal.name: Nightly test self-healing
nightly-test-heal.description: Run tests every night and attempt minimal fixes for failures in an isolated worktree
nightly-test-heal.prompt:
Run the project's test suite. If there are failures, attempt a minimal fix in an isolated worktree.
Constraints:
- Determine the standard test command from the repo docs or package scripts before running the full suite
- Only fix issues backed by clear failing evidence; prefer the smallest possible change and avoid drive-by refactoring
- Re-run the affected tests after fixing to confirm they pass, and review the full diff
- Deliver fixes through the repo's workflow (e.g. create a branch and open a PR); never commit directly to the main branch
- For failures that cannot be fixed safely, report the cause, suspicious files, and suggested next steps

pr-gatekeeper.name: PR gatekeeper
pr-gatekeeper.description: Pre-review new changes on open PRs each weekday and report risks by severity
pr-gatekeeper.prompt:
Review the repository's open PRs and pre-screen their new changes.
Constraints:
- Go through open PRs with new commits in the past 24 hours (on Monday, look back over the whole weekend), citing PR numbers, file paths, and concrete diffs
- Focus on correctness, security, data-loss, and compatibility issues, graded by severity
- Only report issues backed by evidence and describe the failure scenario; do not nitpick on style preferences
- Unless explicitly authorized, only output review conclusions; do not comment on PRs or change code

domain-radar.name: Domain radar
domain-radar.description: Periodically collect the latest updates in a topic you follow and deliver an opinionated digest
domain-radar.prompt:
Collect the latest developments about "{{topic}}" from the past 24 hours (on Monday, look back over the whole weekend) and produce an opinionated digest.
Constraints:
- Use web search, cross-check multiple sources before trusting a claim, and cite the source link for every item
- Prefer substantive developments (releases, research, policy, notable discussions); filter out marketing fluff and reposts
- For each item, add a one-line judgement on why it matters instead of dumping links
- When information is scarce or sources are questionable, say so honestly; never fabricate

competitor-watch.name: Competitor watch
competitor-watch.description: Weekly roundup of competitors' product and market moves, with impact analysis
competitor-watch.prompt:
Track the past week's activity of these competitors: {{competitors}}.
Constraints:
- Use web search to cover product updates, releases, pricing changes, market moves, and user sentiment, citing sources
- Distinguish official information from third-party accounts; clearly mark unverified rumors
- For each significant update, analyze what it means for us and suggest a response
- If nothing substantive happened, say so honestly instead of padding the report

weekly-work-draft.name: Weekly report drafter
weekly-work-draft.description: Compile this week's work from documents in the working directory into a report draft
weekly-work-draft.prompt:
Based on this week's changes to documents, notes, and deliverables in the working directory, compile a weekly report draft.
Constraints:
- Only use content with actual modification traces in the working directory as evidence, citing the files
- Organize as "Done this week / In progress / Next week / Needs coordination", concise enough to submit directly
- Separate substantive progress from routine chores and highlight valuable output
- Leave placeholders with notes where the material is insufficient so the user can fill them in

knowledge-freshness.name: Knowledge base freshness check
knowledge-freshness.description: Monthly health check of working-directory docs for outdated or conflicting content
knowledge-freshness.prompt:
Health-check the documents in the working directory and find content that needs updating.
Constraints:
- Look for outdated information (stale dates, dead links, deprecated processes or tools), contradictions, and duplication
- Cite the file path and location for every issue and explain the reasoning
- Categorize as "update / merge / delete" suggestions and produce a revision checklist
- Only output the report; do not modify the documents

Help me turn it into a complete, clear GitHub issue: confirm whether it is a bug or feature request, and ask only for missing or ambiguous details. This task switched model midway, and Codex still evaluates the context limit against the previous model. Switch back to that model to continue, or start a new task.
errors.turnNoEventTimeout: This turn showed no activity for a long time (model, tools and background processes were all silent), so it was interrupted to avoid hanging forever. Send the next message to continue.
